listenings.text: Every week someone comes to my desk and tells me the same thing. I used to read all the time, but now I simply haven't got the time. And I always ask: what was the last book you really enjoyed? Usually it was years ago. So here's my advice. Don't start with a classic. Start with a page-turner, something with short chapters and a good plot twist. A mystery, a thriller, a funny novel. And don't wait for a free afternoon, because it isn't coming. Read ten pages a day, on the commute, or in bed before you drift off. Within a month, most people come back and say they got hooked again.

For years, my commute was an hour each way. Two hours a day on a crowded train. I was always checking emails or reading the news on my phone, and I arrived at work already tired. Then one day a colleague gave me a detective novel. She had finished it the week before and she said, you'll love it. I didn't believe her. But I started it on the train home, and by the time I got to my station, I had read sixty pages. Since then, the train is my reading room. I've read more books in the last two years than in the ten years before.

People ask me how to write a page-turner, and I tell them there are three secrets. First, every chapter ends with a question. Not a big cliffhanger every time, just a small question in the reader's head. What was in the letter? Who had called her? Second, the characters. If the reader doesn't care about them, nothing else works. And third, the plot twist. I always plan it before I write the first page. When I write chapter one, I already know what is going to happen in chapter twelve. The reader doesn't. That's the fun part.

paras: It was raining when Rafael left the office that Thursday. He had spent ten hours in front of a screen full of numbers, and his head was still full of market news. Like every night, he was standing on a crowded train, holding his phone, when he noticed an old paperback on the seat next to him. Someone had left it there. He picked it up only to avoid the news on his phone. He did not expect anything from it.

By the third station, he had forgotten about the rat race. The novel was a page-turner. The main character, a woman called Ana, was looking for a brother she had never met, and every chapter ended with a question. Rafael got hooked so fast that he almost missed his stop. He had not felt like that about a book since he was a teenager, when his friends used to call him a bookworm.

That night he could not switch off the story. He was still reading at two in the morning, and he drifted off with the book open on his chest. The next day, his commute felt different. While the other passengers were checking the market, he was reading. In chapter twelve there was a plot twist that he had not seen coming at all. He smiled. Somebody had left him the best way to unwind, on a seat, on a Thursday.
